sources.news_title: Jewish TV star Adam Brody calls Israeli actions in Gaza ‘genocide’
sources.text:
Adam Brody, who stars as a rabbi in the Netflix rom-com series Nobody Wants This, for the first time publicly shared his view that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.
“Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” Brody said in a new interview with GQ. “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.”
Brody said he has spoken about his opinions on Israel privately, but until now had not “spoken much about it publicly.” He added that he hoped for another presidential administration to “correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is.”
Brody sees growing 'conservative' views in Hollywood
The Jewish actor plays Los Angeles-based rabbi Noah Roklov in the hit Netflix show, which returns for a third season on Oct. 22. It’s the latest in a string of Jewish roles that made him famous, including Seth Cohen in The OC and Seth Morris in Fleishman Is in Trouble. In real life, Brody has said he is an atheist who “barely got bar mitzvah'd and retained nothing from it.”
Brody told GQ that the Gaza war, alongside other national and global crises, has revealed “more conservative” views among his Hollywood peers in recent years.
“Between COVID, a second Trump term, Israel-Gaza, it’s really brought out some different beliefs that I was ignorant of, and then disheartened by,” he said.
Israel’s actions in Gaza have divided the entertainment industry. While celebrities such as Jerry Seinfeld, Gal Gadot and Amy Schumer have voiced support for Israel since the Hamas attacks on October 7, 2023, other Jewish actors have said that Israel is guilty of genocide in the retaliation that followed, including Hannah Einbinder and Wallace Shawn. Einbinder was among about 100 people arrested during a protest against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City.
The genocide accusation is heavily disputed. A United Nations Commission of Inquiry, along with international and Israeli human rights groups, has concluded that Israel’s actions in Gaza fit that description. However, the International Court of Justice has not yet issued a final judgment on allegations of genocide brought by South Africa against Israel.
Israel has strongly rejected the accusation. Netanyahu, in his UN address last week, called it “the greatest lie of the 21st century,” saying that Israel “prevented genocide” by protecting Palestinians in Gaza while Hamas “used Palestinian civilians as human shields.”
Brody, Netflix, and representatives from Nobody Wants This did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Brody, who plays rabbi Noah Roklov opposite Kristen Bell’s agnostic podcaster in Netflix’s series Nobody Wants This, now wants everybody to know that he is for a “free Palestine.” “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide,” Brody stated said unequivocally. “Put me down as wanting a free Palestine. It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago… I’m not trying to plead ignorance—here we are doing a political interview, so it makes sense that we wade into this territory—but I’ve never ducked a question, really, not a political question anyway.”
  
The actor, a longtime Democrat and voting rights advocate, noted that he’s not generally one to put his politics front and center in celebrity appearances, although the issue comes up “a lot” in his private life. Continuing, Brody stated, “I just answer the questions I’m asked. And it’s true. I’m not wearing a pin, so I’m not inviting a certain question, and perhaps I should. I really admire people who do.” 
Brody, who’s also not on any social media, defended his usual code of silence, stating, “I think being off social media has been the healthiest thing. I’m forced to use a lot of tools and products where I don’t believe in the heads of those companies, but I’m sure as shit not going to be on anything that Elon Musk is a part of.” 
 
The third season of Nobody Wants This premieres October 22 on Netflix.

“I just answer the questions I’m asked,” the actor told GQ. “And it’s true. I’m not wearing a pin, so I’m not inviting a certain question, and perhaps I should. I really admire people who do. I’m not trying to plead ignorance—here we are doing a political interview, so it makes sense that we wade into this territory—but I’ve never ducked a question, really, not a political question anyway.”
The “O.C.” actor explained that while he hadn’t spoken publicly about the Israel-Gaza issue before, it comes up “a lot” for him in private. He then made his stance on the conflict clear: “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide,” he said. “Put me down as wanting a free Palestine. It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.”
Popular on Variety
Brody, who isn’t on social media, also defended his decision to remain offline. “I think being off social media has been the healthiest thing. I’m forced to use a lot of tools and products where I don’t believe in the heads of those companies, but I’m sure as shit not going to be on anything that Elon Musk is a part of,” he said. “I know people are doing really good work on [X], and I’m really glad about that. But it’s not for me, and I don’t have any guilt about not being on it. Sorry, I feel great about it.”
Brody has starred in Netflix’s romantic comedy series “Nobody Wants This” as rabbi Noah Roklov since Season 1 premiered in 2024. Season 3 is due on the streamer on Oct. 22.

sources.news_title: Adam Brody describes Gaza war as ‘genocide’
sources.text:
Adam Brody, the Jewish actor who plays a rabbi in the Netflix series Nobody Wants This, has described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “genocide”.
In an interview with US men’s magazine GQ, he said: “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide.
“Put me down as wanting a free Palestine. It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.
“I’m hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is.”
Brody joins other prominent Jewish actors in accusing Israel of genocide, including Hannah Einbinder and Ilana Glazer.
His comments came as a surprise to many observers partly because he had previously kept his feelings about the war private, and does not maintain a public social media presence.
Brody also spoke about what he saw as Hollywood’s conservatism, saying: “Between COVID, a second Trump term, Israel-Gaza, it’s really brought out some different beliefs that I was ignorant to, and then disheartened by.”
Despite being Jewish, the 46-year-old told the Los Angeles Times ahead of the premiere of Nobody Wants This in 2024: “I didn’t know the first thing about Judaism.”
“I initially winced at the religiosity of it,” he said. “But I came around to being excited by that aspect and going, ‘Well, that’s the different part than me, and that’s what will be fun stuff to research and explore and commit to and play.’”
More than 5,000 public figures two weeks ago signed an open letter rejecting allegations that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.
The letter, released by Creative Community for Peace (CCFP), suggested that the allegation of genocide unfairly targets the Jewish State and does not stand up to scrutiny.
The signatories, including actors Debra Messing, Mayim Bialik, Maureen Lipman and Jennifer Jason Leigh, historian Deborah Lipstadt, Disturbed frontman David Draiman, and Mad Men creator Matthew Weiner, dubbed the claim a “blood libel” and a “lie”.

Brody plays a rabbi in Nobody Wants This, the rom-com Netflix series that has put him back in the spotlight. The show is loosely based on creator Erin Foster’s experiences of converting to Judaism after meeting her husband.
The actor spoke to GQ ahead of the show’s season three release about his involvement in local politics ahead of the midterm elections. After admitting he hadn’t said much publicly about the ongoing conflict, Brody told the publication: “Put me down as thinking it's a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine.”
He continued: “It's awful that it's taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it's reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago. I'm hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is.”
Brody also spoke about Hollywood’s conservatism, saying: “Between COVID, a second Trump term, Israel-Gaza, it’s really brought out some different beliefs that I was ignorant to, and then disheartened by.”
Nobody Wants This follows agnostic sex podcaster Joanne (Kristen Bell), who falls in love with newly single rabbi Noah (Brody). It was renewed for a second season within two weeks of its 2024 premiere. Season three is slated for an October 22 release.
Fans were immediately charmed by Brody’s portrayal of the rabbi, a role he wasn’t sure he was going to take on at first.
Despite being Jewish, the 46-year-old told the Los Angeles Times ahead of the show’s premiere: “I didn’t know the first thing about Judaism.”
“I initially winced at the religiosity of it,” he said. “But I came around to being excited by that aspect and going, ‘Well, that’s the different part than me, and that’s what will be fun stuff to research and explore and commit to and play.’”
The Critics Choice Award winner’s comments come days after several Hollywood stars were detained outside of the United Nations General Assembly in New York City as part of a planned protest while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered remarks.
Hacks star and Emmy winner Hannah Einbinder and Thelma & Louise actor Susan Sarandon were among those detained, per the New York Post. It’s unclear if they face charges.
A massive crowd gathered Thursday ahead of Netanyahu’s planned speech as part of an anti-war sit-in protest outside the U.N. organized by Jewish Voice for Peace. Photos showed celebrities and personalities — including Sex and the City star Cynthia Nixon, whistleblower Chelsea Manning and comedian Caleb Heron — among hundreds in attendance. sources.news_title: Ahead of ‘Nobody Wants This’ Season 3, Adam Brody Declares His Support for “A Free Palestine”
sources.text:
Nobody Wants This star Adam Brody is sharing his thoughts on the ongoing Israel-Gaza war, telling GQ in a new interview that he is in support of “a free Palestine.”
The actor, who appears on the Netflix series as a rabbi, discussed his political activism with GQ, and was asked if he thinks Hollywood has gotten more conservative. “I guess outspokenly so, yes. Again, as one side has more power, it makes sense that it draws people to it for all the human reasons that would be attractive: groupthink, your own well-being, your own money and success,” he said.
Brody continued, “Between COVID, a second Trump term, Israel-Gaza, it’s really brought out some different beliefs that I was ignorant to, and then disheartened by.”
The interviewer asked the actor how Israel-Gaza has come up in his messaging, to which he responded, “Truthfully, it hasn’t. I have spoken a lot about it privately. I haven’t spoken much about it publicly.”
When asked if he’d like to speak about the topic, The O.C. actor said, “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine.”
“It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago,” he continued. “I’m hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is.”
Netflix is gearing up to release the third season of its Jewish rom-com Nobody Wants This on Oct. 22. Brody was nominated for a 2025 Emmy for his role in the series, and won the Critics Choice Award for best comedy actor that same year.
Last year, during an interview for Variety‘s Actors on Actors series in June, Brody said Nobody Wants This was a “safe, celebratory space” amid a “sensitive time.”
“I think right now is a particularly sensitive time for literally everyone, but certainly Jewish people,” he said. “And I think this [show] being a sort of safe, celebratory space for it has been very well received.”
In an August 2025 interview with The Hollywood Reporter, series creator Erin Foster said of the show, “It was really important to me and continues to be really important to tell positive Jewish stories. I know that it can be polarizing, but it shouldn’t be. This is not the show to tackle conflict in Israel and Palestine.”
“I’m not the person to tell that story,” Foster added. “And after [the attacks on] Oct. 7 happened, there were conversations around if we were going to dive into it, and the truth is, the way that I can get my message across best is by shedding a positive light on Jewish characters and Jewish traditions. I don’t think somebody watching wants to see another voice give you their opinion on what’s happening.”

sources.text:
‘Nobody Wants This’ star Adam Brody on Gaza: ‘Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide’
Brody, who plays a rabbi on the hit Netflix rom-com, has not previously made public statements about the war
Adam Brody, the Jewish actor who plays a “hot rabbi” on the hit Netflix rom-com Nobody Wants This, called the war in Gaza a genocide in a new interview, making him one of just a few Jewish celebrities to speak out publicly against the Israeli campaign.
The comments came in an interview with GQ about Brody’s efforts canvassing for Democratic candidates in the upcoming midterms.
“Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” he said. “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago. I’m hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is.”
The claim of genocide in Gaza is heavily disputed. Several international bodies, human rights organizations and academic institutions have concluded Israel’s actions in Gaza since Oct. 7 fit the description, including a United Nations Commission of Inquiry. Other similar groups, like the International Court of Justice, have not applied the term.
Brody’s comments were surprising in part because he had previously kept his feelings about the war private, even as other leading Hollywood figures openly criticized it. He does not maintain a public social media presence, and he did not participate in pin-wearing campaigns or sign various petitions related to the war — an approach he indicated he might change going forward.
“I’m not wearing a pin, so I’m not inviting a certain question, and perhaps I should,” he said. “I really admire people who do. But 99% of what I’m asked about is about the show. I’m not trying to plead ignorance—here we are doing a political interview, so it makes sense that we wade into this territory—but I’ve never ducked a question, really, not a political question anyway.”
Brody — who came to fame in the 2000s as the teenager Seth Cohen on The O.C. — joins Hacks star Hannah Einbinder and Wallace Shawn (The Princess Bride) as perhaps the most high-profile Jewish actors to publicly call the war a genocide. Other Jewish entertainment figures, like Mandy Patinkin and The Zone of Interest director Jonathan Glazer, have criticized the war but stopped short of calling it a genocide.
Yet Brody’s comments are perhaps especially notable because of the character he plays on TV. In Nobody Wants This, Brody plays a rabbi dating a non-Jewish woman — introducing her to the beauty and foibles of Jewish faith and culture. Israel has been conspicuously absent from the show, with its creator, Erin Foster, saying she deliberately avoided geopolitics.
Season 3 of Nobody Wants This releases to Netflix October 22.

It’s a stance he says he’s talked through often in private, though he’d never voiced it publicly before now.
“It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery,” he said, “but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.”

The show, for the record, is Netflix’s Nobody Wants This, in which Brody plays rabbi Noah Roklov. Its first season premiered in 2024, and Season 3 is due on Netflix Oct. 22, 2026.
Speaking his mind publicly is one thing; doing it on social media is another. Brody acknowledged that people do valuable work on X, but said he won’t join a platform involving Elon Musk. In fact, he stays off social media entirely, and called being off it “the healthiest thing.”
“It’s not for me, and I don’t have any guilt about not being on it,” Brody said. “Sorry, I feel great about it.”

sources.news_title: America’s Progressives Demand a Multi Ethnic Israel but Tolerate an Arab Muslim Palestine
sources.text:
America’s Progressives Demand a Multi-Ethnic Israel, Tolerate an Arab Muslim Palestine
From Adam Brody’s “Free Palestine” declaration to Peter Beinart and Jon Stewart, one question remains remarkably neglected: What kind of Palestine are progressives actually advocating?
By Hussain Abdul-Hussain
This week, Adam Brody became the latest prominent American celebrity to board the “Free Palestine” train. In a September 25 interview with GQ, the actor offered a blunt assessment of the war in Gaza: “Put me down as thinking it's a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine.” Read Brody’s GQ interview
He is hardly alone. A day earlier, actors Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder were among demonstrators detained outside the United Nations during a protest against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, another sign of how thoroughly the Palestinian cause has moved into the center of progressive American culture.
But beneath the increasingly fashionable slogan lies a question that is almost never asked: Free Palestine to become what?
An enormous blind spot has come to dominate the discourse of certain progressive Jewish-American commentators, most notably figures like Peter Beinart and Jon Stewart. Beinart has gone considerably further than Stewart, explicitly abandoning the two-state model in favor of a single political framework based on equal citizenship for Jews and Palestinians, while Stewart has provided one of America’s most influential platforms for a broader progressive critique of Israel. The two sat together on The Daily Show in 2025 for an extended discussion of Gaza, Judaism, Israel and Palestinian rights.
While their arguments are presented as an unyielding defense of liberal democratic values, their prescriptions for the Middle East contain a profound structural contradiction. The explicitly Jewish character of Israel is subjected to relentless scrutiny, and in Beinart’s case rejected as incompatible with genuine equality. Yet far less attention is paid to a Palestinian national movement that openly envisions its future state as Arab in national identity and Muslim in important elements of its constitutional character.
This inexplicable bias mirrors a broader cultural phenomenon in the West: a performative eagerness to replace traditional Western or Judeo-Christian cultural markers with secular, bland alternatives while going out of the way to loudly celebrate non-Western traditions. On Christmas and Hanukkah, the politically correct greeting is a generic “happy holidays.” On Islamic holidays, the politically correct greeting is the Arabic “Eid Mubarak.”
While these commentators believe their positions are steeped in fairness, ethics and universal humanity, their advocacy is frequently driven by an uncritical romanticization of the global non-West. By viewing what they perceive as “indigenous” or “native” cultures through a lens of unalloyed sentimentality, they treat Western institutional traditions as uniquely flawed while remaining strikingly incurious about the illiberal realities governing the societies they seek to empower.
On the domestic front, the progressive blueprint is exhaustive. The likes of Beinart and Stewart present a long list of injustices they demand to see fixed in America, championing gender equality, LGBTQ rights, the rule of law and robust social safety nets. These demands apply to Israel too. Yet when attention shifts to the Arab world, a different instinct frequently emerges: authoritarian governments, sectarian social structures and illiberal institutions become matters that outsiders are warned not to impose themselves upon.
America’s progressives rarely discuss Palestinians as a society that itself requires structural transformation regarding the rights of women, the protection of sexual minorities or the establishment of independent democratic institutions. The Palestinian struggle is instead reduced primarily to the mechanical concession of land and power. What happens to the Palestinian population after the borders are drawn is too often treated as an afterthought.
Geopolitical vacuums, however, are never filled by abstract liberal ideals. They are filled by the most organized, heavily armed and illiberal factions available. When a Palestinian is the tragic victim of an Israeli bullet, it can become an international crisis. Yet when Palestinians are imprisoned, silenced or killed by Hamas or other Palestinian factions, comparable international attention is often much harder to find.
It is easy to champion vogue, contrarian ideas when one has grown up in the security and prosperity of American suburbs. It is quite another to understand the harrowing reality of living inside a failing state.
My perspective on this matter does not come from academic theory, but from lived experience. I grew up in a dual-national, Iraqi-Lebanese household. In that environment, national identity was never engraved in stone; it was a fluid asset negotiable for survival. My family moved between Baghdad and Beirut to escape endless sectarian conflicts, constantly seeking whichever nation could offer a temporary semblance of stability.
In my adulthood, I continued this search for a better life and migrated to the United States, where I was naturalized and fully assimilated. Today, I consider myself a patriotic American. I carry the rich heritage of my ancestral homelands proudly, but my political allegiance belongs exclusively to the American republic.
Living as a national in both Iraq and Lebanon meant living within states that conceptualized public space through a singular, majoritarian lens. As a Muslim-born Arab, my cultural identity naturally aligned with much of the dominant apparatus of the state. Moving to America changed that dynamic completely. Unlike the traditional nation-states of the Old World, America largely decouples cultural identity from national belonging.
What determines an individual’s Americanism is not blood, faith or ancestral lineage, but a shared commitment to the Constitution and the founding principles of the republic.
While American identity was undeniably shaped by the Judeo-Christian traditions of its founders, the structural separation of church and state remains one of its cornerstones. English acts as the de facto language of governance, yet it seamlessly coexists with Spanish and dozens of other languages depending on the region.
This multi-ethnic civic model is historically unusual. Many nations around the world, including mature Western democracies such as France or Denmark, retain strong cultural, linguistic and historical identities tied to a majority nation. This majoritarian structure becomes significantly more pronounced in the Middle East, where public space in many countries is explicitly Arab and Islamic. Iraq features Allahu Akbar on its national flag. Syria’s official designation remains the Syrian Arab Republic, despite the presence of Kurds, Assyrians and other minorities.
And this is where the debate over Palestine becomes particularly revealing.
The February 2026 draft constitution for the State of Palestine leaves little ambiguity about the national character being envisioned. It declares that Palestine is part of the Arab homeland and that the Palestinian Arab people are part of the Arab nation. Islam is the official religion, the principles of Islamic Sharia are designated a primary source of legislation, and Arabic is the official language.
To be accurate, the same constitution also declares Palestine a representative parliamentary democracy, promises equality among citizens and explicitly states that the rights of Christians are respected. The issue is therefore not that Palestinian constitutional texts formally deny non-Muslims citizenship. It is that Palestine is emphatically not being envisioned as the culturally neutral, post-national state that some Western progressives increasingly demand Israel become.
Palestinians are being encouraged to exercise Arab national self-determination. Jews are increasingly told that exercising Jewish national self-determination is itself the problem.
That contradiction becomes even more striking when examining Israel as it actually exists. Israel defines itself as a Jewish state, but more than two million Arab citizens participate in its political system, form parties, serve in the Knesset and debate how best to influence the direction of the country. As a recent Mid.East Journal analysis of Arab voters in Israel’s 2026 election showed, Arab citizens can maintain Palestinian, Arab, religious and Israeli components of identity simultaneously while participating directly in Israeli politics.
The question, then, is not whether Palestinians are entitled to national identity. Of course they are. The question is why Palestinian Arab nationalism is treated as the legitimate fulfillment of self-determination while Jewish nationalism is increasingly portrayed by the same intellectual circles as an obstacle to equality.
The history of minorities in the region makes this question more than theoretical. Once-flourishing Jewish communities across Iraq, Egypt, Yemen and Libya virtually disappeared during the twentieth century, while Christian communities in countries such as Iraq and Syria have suffered dramatic demographic decline through combinations of persecution, war, instability and emigration. The history of the region’s ancient Jewish communities is worth remembering precisely because Jews were not foreign arrivals to the Middle East; communities existed across the region for centuries before their near disappearance in the modern era. Mid.East Journal: Where Are Jews From?
That history does not prove that a future Palestinian state must repeat the failures of Iraq, Syria or Yemen. But it should explain why Israelis might be skeptical of arguments that national sovereignty can simply be surrendered on the assumption that liberal pluralism will inevitably emerge afterward.
There is a profound irony in the geopolitical debate I am engaging in here: a Muslim-born Arab immigrant like me finds himself defending the necessity of a secure, sovereign Jewish state against the destabilizing idealism of Western commentators who demand that Jewish national identity meet a standard they rarely impose on the surrounding region.
True introspection requires looking inward to address the historic failures of Arab and Islamic governance regarding pluralism, institutional stability and minority rights.
Palestinian self-determination cannot be evaluated only by asking how much territory Palestinians should control. We should also ask what institutions will govern that territory, what protections its minorities will enjoy and whether the political culture being constructed can sustain the liberal values its Western advocates claim to champion.
Progressive advocacy must confront the Middle East as it actually is, rather than as it appears from the safety of the West.
If liberalism requires Israel to transcend Jewish nationalism, its advocates should at least explain why Palestinian Arab nationalism is asked to make no comparable journey.
Hussain Abdul-Hussain is the author of The Arab Case for Israel. He is a research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD). He is a frequent contributor to Mideast.Journal.

sources.news_title: Adam Brody, The Jewish Actor Behind Rabbi Noah, Says He Wants “A Free Palestine”
sources.text:
Adam Brody is about to return to Netflix as the charming rabbi at the center of Nobody Wants This. But off-screen, the Jewish actor is talking about something far heavier.
Ahead of Season 3, Brody has publicly described Israel’s war on Gaza as a “genocide” and said he wants “a free Palestine” — a striking shift from keeping his views largely private.
It is also a particularly notable stance coming from an actor whose most prominent recent role is that of Rabbi Noah Roklov, a Jewish rabbi navigating faith, love and an interfaith relationship.
“Put Me Down As Wanting A Free Palestine”
In a new GQ interview, Brody said he had spoken extensively about Gaza in private but had largely stayed quiet publicly.
This time, when given the opportunity to speak, he didn’t hedge:
“Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine. It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago. I’m hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is.”
There is a sense of frustration running through his words — not only at the scale of the suffering, but at how long it has taken for the conversation around it to reach what he sees as a breaking point.
The Rabbi On Netflix, The Activist Off-Screen
For many viewers, Brody will always be Seth Cohen — the sarcastic, comic-book-loving teenager he played on The O.C..
Seth was also Jewish, making Brody’s later role as Rabbi Noah more than just another Jewish character in his filmography. Years after The O.C., he would step into a very different kind of Jewish role: a rabbi whose faith is central to his love story.
Brody himself was born to Jewish parents with family roots in Russia and Poland. He has previously described Nobody Wants This as a “safe, celebratory space” for Jewish people during a particularly sensitive period.
A Jewish Actor Speaking Out
That context gives his latest comments another layer.
Brody joins prominent Jewish actors including Hannah Einbinder and Wallace Shawn in publicly condemning Israel’s actions in Gaza.
And while he says he has discussed the issue privately for some time, he is now putting his own position firmly on the record — as a Jewish actor whose most recognizable roles have both been deeply tied to Jewish identity.
Why Now?
The timing adds another layer.
Brody’s comments come just weeks before Nobody Wants This returns for Season 3 on October 22. They also arrive as Hollywood’s relationship with the Israel-Gaza war continues to play out publicly, with actors including Einbinder and Susan Sarandon recently detained during a protest outside the United Nations during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit.
For Brody, though, this isn’t entirely new. He says he has been talking about the issue privately for years.
What is new is putting those words on the record.
Before The Rom-Com Returns
Soon, Brody will once again be on screen as Rabbi Noah, the fictional rabbi viewers fell for.
But before Season 3 arrives, he has made one thing very real: his own position on Gaza — and his support for a free Palestine — is no longer something he is keeping to himself.

sources.news_title: Adam Brody Breaks His Public Silence on Gaza Ahead of ‘Nobody Wants This’ Season 3
sources.text:
Adam Brody Breaks His Public Silence on Gaza Ahead of ‘Nobody Wants This’ Season 3
Adam Brody has become one of streaming’s most beloved leading men thanks to his role as Rabbi Noah Roklov, and his profile is only set to climb as the Netflix hit gears up for its return. Now, Adam Brody’s Gaza comments are drawing just as much attention as the show itself, marking a notable shift for an actor who has largely kept his politics out of the spotlight.
‘Nobody Wants This’, created by Erin Foster, follows the relationship between Brody’s Noah and Joanne, an agnostic podcaster played by Kristen Bell. The mixed-faith rom-com has earned Brody 2 Golden Globe nominations, along with a 2025 Emmy nomination and a Critics’ Choice Award for best comedy actor.
In a new interview with GQ focused on his political views, Brody addressed the Israel-Gaza war publicly for what appears to be the first time. The actor said he considers the war a genocide and declared his support for a free Palestine.
He added that it’s awful that it has taken so much death and misery, but said the situation feels like it is reaching a breaking point that should have come long ago. Brody also expressed hope that a future U.S. administration could do some good and change course.
Asked why he hadn’t addressed the issue before, Brody explained that the topic simply hadn’t come up in his recent interviews. He noted he has spoken about it extensively in private but rarely in public, and said nearly all red-carpet questions focus on ‘Nobody Wants This’.
The conversation also touched on whether Hollywood has become more conservative, which Brody agreed has happened in outspoken ways. He suggested that when one side holds more power, people are drawn toward it for very human reasons, including groupthink, personal well-being, money, and success.
Brody said the combination of COVID, a second Trump term, and the Israel-Gaza war revealed beliefs he had been unaware of and then felt disheartened by. The Jerusalem Post-affiliated outlet Ynet noted that the Jewish actor is one of relatively few Jewish celebrities to speak out publicly against Israel’s campaign in this way.
As with most statements on the conflict, the response has been sharply divided. Some social media users praised Brody for using his platform, while others questioned the timing, with one reply cynically suggesting the comments were tied to the upcoming season’s promotion.
Kristen Bell and Adam Brody star in the first trailer for #NobodyWantsThis: Season 3.
The new season premieres October 22 on Netflix. pic.twitter.com/uTBJzZZ1b7
Other responses were openly hostile, reflecting how polarizing the subject remains. Several outlets noted that Brody’s comments represent his personal view rather than a settled consensus, as the genocide characterization is strongly disputed by Israel and its supporters.
The interview arrived shortly after around 100 people, including several of Brody’s Hollywood peers, were arrested outside the United Nations General Assembly in New York while protesting the arrival of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Despite the attention, ‘Nobody Wants This’ itself isn’t expected to wade into the conflict. In a 2025 interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Foster explained that telling positive Jewish stories remains important to her, while stressing that the series is not the place to tackle the conflict in Israel and Palestine.
Season 3 follows Noah and Joanne as they move in together and navigate a new stage of their relationship. Andrew Rannells, Keyla Monterroso Mejia, and Sarah Silverman join the cast in recurring roles.
All 10 episodes of the new season premiere on Netflix on October 22. It remains to be seen whether Brody’s remarks will affect how audiences receive the show, but they have clearly added a new dimension to its promotional run.

sources.text:

Again, as one side has more power, it makes sense that it draws people to it for all the human reasons that would be attractive: groupthink, your own well-being, your own money and success,” he said.
Brody added, “Between COVID, a second Trump term, Israel-Gaza, it’s really brought out some different beliefs that I was ignorant to, and then disheartened by.”
He admitted that “truthfully,” the Israel-Hamas war has not come up for him in recent interviews, despite his role as Rabbi Noah Roklov in the Erin Foster-created series. “I have spoken a lot about it privately. I haven’t spoken much about it publicly,” he noted.
“Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” Brody continued. “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago. I’m hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is.”
In “Nobody Wants This,” agnostic podcaster Joanne Williams (Kristen Bell) begins an unexpected romance with Rabbi Noah Roklov (Brody), which shakes both their families as Joanne immerses herself in Noah’s culture and decides to convert to Judaism.

sources.text:
‘Nobody Wants This’ Star Adam Brody Calls Gaza War ‘a Genocide’
Adam Brody has spent the past year and a half enjoying a career resurgence few could have predicted, transforming his role as a charming rabbi on Netflix’s ‘Nobody Wants This‘ into one of the most talked-about performances of the streaming era. That newfound platform has come with an unusual amount of scrutiny, given how directly his character intersects with questions of faith and Jewish identity.
Brody has generally kept his personal political views separate from that public-facing role, even as conversations around Israel and Gaza have grown increasingly unavoidable across Hollywood. That reticence changed this week, with the actor addressing the war directly for what appears to be the first time in a public setting.
Speaking with GQ ahead of ‘Nobody Wants This’ Season 3, Brody was asked directly about his views on the conflict and didn’t hold back. “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” he said, according to comments reported by The Hollywood Reporter.
Brody expanded on that stance, framing the ongoing devastation as something that should have reached a turning point long ago. “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago,” he continued. “I’m hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is.”
Prior to this interview, Brody acknowledged he’d largely avoided discussing the war publicly, despite having strong private opinions on the matter. When asked how the conflict had factored into his broader political activism, he was candid about that gap. “Truthfully, it hasn’t,” he said. “I have spoken a lot about it privately. I haven’t spoken much about it publicly.”
That admission adds context to why his comments have drawn particular attention. Brody plays Rabbi Noah Roklov in the Erin Foster-created series, a role that’s made him one of the more visible Jewish figures on television, which makes his willingness to speak out notable regardless of where audiences land on the underlying politics.
The characterization of Israel’s military campaign as a genocide remains a contested and widely disputed claim, with different international bodies, governments and commentators offering sharply divergent assessments of the conflict. Brody’s comments reflect his personal view on the matter rather than a settled consensus, and they arrive amid a broader wave of Hollywood figures speaking out on the subject in recent weeks.
Brody’s remarks follow a string of similar statements from other prominent entertainment figures. Actors including Hannah Einbinder and Wallace Shawn have previously used the word genocide to describe the conflict, while others such as Mandy Patinkin have criticized the war without going that far in their language.
The timing also coincides with heightened protest activity in the industry, including a demonstration outside the United Nations General Assembly in New York, where roughly 100 people, including Einbinder and Susan Sarandon, were detained while protesting the arrival of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
“It’s perfect because it’s us.”

With ‘Nobody Wants This’ Season 3 set to premiere on Netflix on October 22, Brody’s comments arrive at a moment when his public profile is set to climb even higher. Whether his remarks affect how audiences receive the new season remains to be seen, but they mark a clear shift from an actor who’d previously kept this particular topic close to the vest.
